title: GPX Duration Calculator: Elapsed Track Time
description: Compute a GPX track's recorded duration from its earliest and latest timestamps with the GPX Duration Calculator. Free, in your browser.
summary_sentence: For example, a track stamped from 07:00:00Z to 11:24:36Z lasted 4 hours, 24 minutes and 36 seconds of elapsed time — pauses, photos and all.
quick_answer: The GPX Duration Calculator reads the earliest and latest timestamps in a GPX file and reports the elapsed time between them — the recording's full span on the clock. Load the file locally and read the duration — the denominator behind averages and 'how long were we out there?'

A device that died mid-hike shows a duration shorter than the day. Comparing span against the plan finds where the record stops.
Files spanning midnight or merged days produce nonsense averages downstream. Checking durations first is the cheap gate.
Race and challenge recordings prove participation partly by their span — the elapsed window is the first fact an organiser reads.

Latest 11:24:36Z minus earliest 07:00:00Z = 15,876 seconds = 4:24:36. Every duration figure is endpoint arithmetic; the calculator's care goes into finding the true earliest and latest stamps wherever they hide in the file.

A watch left running in the car park can stretch a 2-hour ride into a 9-hour 'duration'. The number is correct about the file and wrong about the ride — the distinction this page's framing keeps in view.

popular_table.intro: Three time quantities a GPX file supports — do not let them impersonate each other.
rows: Latest stamp minus earliest stamp — wall clock, pauses included
Time above a speed threshold — device-defined, file-interpreted
The same endpoint window, reported as start/end instants (the Timestamp Span Calculator's framing)
Sum of segment spans when the recorder slept between segments
popular_table.note: GPX timestamps are UTC (the Z suffix) per the format's convention — durations are timezone-proof precisely because both endpoints live in the same frame.

faq: What if some trackpoints lack timestamps?
Points without <time> are ignored for the span; the duration is computed from the stamps that exist. A file with fewer than two stamps has no duration to give.
The elapsed span includes the gap — that is what elapsed means. Per-segment spans are visible in the file's structure; splitting the file is the fix for separate outings.
GPX stamps are UTC, so DST never enters the subtraction. Your local display of the start time may shift; the duration cannot.
Only in a corrupt file (stamps out of order). The calculator takes earliest-to-latest regardless of document order, so a shuffled file still yields its true span — disorder is reported, not obeyed.
Stamps commonly carry whole seconds; some devices write fractional seconds, and the span honours them.
Planned routes rarely carry real stamps; where they do, the same endpoint arithmetic applies, labelled as the plan's window rather than a recording's.
